chapters.title: Chapter 5: Analysing Performance Like a Manager

lessons.title: Capex vs Opex: How Your Spending Decisions Show Up in the Statements

children.text: Your team needs 300 laptops. You can buy them outright for ₹1.8 crore, or take them on a managed subscription at ₹2,200 per device a month. Same machines on the same desks. One route goes on the balance sheet and is charged to profit over three years. The other hits this year's profit in full and never appears as an asset.

That choice, capital expenditure or operating expenditure, changes your margins, your ROCE, who has to approve the spend and how your team looks at the next review. This lesson shows exactly what each route does.

body.text: Capex buys an asset and is charged to profit slowly. Opex buys a period of use and is charged now. The cash can be identical and the statements will not be.

children.text: The test is whether the spending creates a resource the company controls that will produce benefit beyond the current period. If yes, it goes on the balance sheet and is depreciated. If no, it is an expense now.

cells: A resource used for years, so it is capitalised and depreciated
Repairing that machine to keep it running
Restores existing performance rather than improving it
Upgrading the machine to raise output by 20%
Enhances the future benefit beyond the original standard
Annual maintenance contract on the machine
Buys a period of service, not an asset
Assets with a useful life of about three years
Subscribing to laptops or software monthly
Buys use for the period, with no asset acquired
Accumulated in capital work in progress until it is ready for use
Salaries of staff who will run the new warehouse
Employee cost of the period, not part of the asset

body.title: What can actually be included in an asset's cost

children.text: Under Ind AS 16, the cost of an item of property, plant and equipment includes more than the invoice value, and less than managers usually assume.

purchase price after trade discounts, import duties and non-refundable taxes, freight and handling, site preparation, installation and assembly, professional fees directly attributable to the asset, and the estimated cost of dismantling and restoring the site.
staff training on the new machine, administrative and general overheads, costs of introducing a new product, relocation costs and initial operating losses while demand builds.

under Ind AS 38, research costs are expensed as incurred. Development costs are capitalised only when the project meets strict tests, including technical feasibility and an intention and ability to complete and use it.
under Ind AS 23, borrowing costs on a qualifying asset that takes a substantial time to get ready can be capitalised into its cost until it is ready for use.
The practical consequence for a project manager: budget the training, trial runs and early losses separately, because they hit this year's P&L even though they belong to a capitalised project.

body.title: Classify the spend
body.question: Kesari Foods spends ₹40 lakh replacing worn conveyor belts on an existing line, keeping output unchanged, and ₹65 lakh adding an automated weighing unit that raises the line's output by 15%. How should each be treated?
options: ₹40 lakh as operating expenditure and ₹65 lakh as capital expenditure
₹40 lakh as capital expenditure and ₹65 lakh as operating expenditure
body.explanation: Replacing parts to maintain existing performance is repairs, so it is expensed. The weighing unit raises output beyond the original standard, so it is capitalised and depreciated over its useful life.

children.text: Once capitalised, an asset is charged to the P&L across its useful life. Schedule II of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes indicative useful lives and companies generally depreciate down to a residual value of 5% of cost.

body.caption: The straight line method, used by most Indian companies
Indicative useful lives under Schedule II

body.title: Work out the annual charge
body.prompt: Kesari Foods buys a machine for ₹90 lakh with a useful life of 15 years and a residual value of 5% of cost, depreciated on a straight line basis. What is the annual depreciation, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Depreciable amount = ₹90 lakh × 95% = ₹85.5 lakh. Divided by 15 years, that is ₹5.7 lakh a year. The full ₹90 lakh left the company in year one as an investing outflow, while the P&L sees only ₹5.7 lakh a year.

body.title: When the clock starts
body.textWithBlank: Depreciation begins when an asset is ready for its intended ___, not when it is first billed or delivered.
body.explanation: Until then the spending sits in capital work in progress, which is why a delayed plant shows a large CWIP balance and no depreciation. Once commissioned, both depreciation and, usually, interest start hitting the P&L together.

children.text: Back to the 300 laptops. Buying costs ₹1.8 crore, depreciated over three years to a 5% residual value, which is ₹57 lakh a year. Subscribing costs ₹2,200 per device a month, which is ₹79.2 lakh a year, or ₹2.38 crore across three years.

body.caption: Buy or subscribe: the same laptops, two routes (₹ lakh)

cells: Charged to the P&L in year one
Nothing, if it qualifies as a low value or short-term arrangement
Effect on capital employed and ROCE
Capital employed up 180.0, so ROCE falls until the assets earn their keep

body.title: Cumulative cash paid over three years (₹ lakh)

stats.label: Extra cash paid to subscribe
stats.context: Over three years, against buying outright

stats.label: EBITDA impact of subscribing
stats.context: A full operating expense every year

body.text: Subscribing costs about ₹58 lakh more in total and still wins in plenty of situations: no upfront cash, no obsolescence risk on three-year-old machines, support and replacement included, and capital employed untouched. The point is not that one route is better. It is that the answer depends on what the company is short of, cash or capital returns, and you should say which.

Be alert to the incentive this creates. A manager measured on EBITDA prefers to capitalise, because depreciation sits below the line. A manager measured on capital employed prefers to lease. Neither preference is about what is best for the company, and finance teams know to test the reasoning when the accounting treatment conveniently suits the person proposing it.

columns.label: Buy (capex)
points: The asset will be used well beyond the payback period
Cheaper in total cash over the asset's life
The company has cash or cheap long-term funding
Technology is stable and obsolescence risk is low
You want the asset available as security for borrowing

columns.label: Subscribe or lease (opex)
points: Cash is tight or better used in working capital
Technology changes quickly, as with laptops and software
Requirement may shrink or change within a few years
Support, replacement and upgrades are bundled in
You want capital employed and ROCE protected

body.title: Buy the ERP or subscribe to it
body.scenario: You head IT at a ₹400 crore revenue auto components maker in Pune. The choice is an on-premise ERP licence at ₹6 crore upfront plus ₹90 lakh a year of maintenance, against a cloud ERP at ₹2.1 crore a year for five years. The CFO has told you the company is close to its interest coverage covenant and is protecting cash.
body.prompt: Compare the two over five years across the statements, and make a recommendation.
body.modelAnswer:
Five-year cash:
1. On-premise: ₹6 crore upfront plus ₹90 lakh a year for five years, which is ₹4.5 crore, giving ₹10.5 crore in total.
2. Cloud: ₹2.1 crore a year for five years, which is ₹10.5 crore in total. On total cash the two are level, so the decision turns on timing and statement effects.
Statement effects:
3. On-premise: ₹6 crore is capitalised as an intangible asset and amortised, say over five years at ₹1.2 crore a year. Cash out in year one is ₹6.9 crore including maintenance. Capital employed rises ₹6 crore, so ROCE falls until benefits arrive. EBITDA carries only the ₹90 lakh of maintenance.
4. Cloud: ₹2.1 crore a year is an operating expense, so EBITDA falls by ₹2.1 crore every year, but capital employed is untouched and year-one cash is ₹2.1 crore instead of ₹6.9 crore.
5. The covenant point: interest coverage uses operating profit over finance costs. Paying ₹6.9 crore upfront almost certainly means borrowing, which raises finance costs and cuts coverage immediately. The cloud route avoids new borrowing.
My recommendation:
6. Cloud, given the stated constraint. Identical total cash, ₹4.8 crore less outflow in year one, no additional debt, and no pressure on the covenant.
7. What I would flag: the cloud cost is contractual for five years and will be repriced at renewal, so negotiate a cap on the annual increase now. Also confirm with finance whether any part of the implementation cost, as opposed to the subscription, qualifies for capitalisation.
8. What would change my mind: if the company had surplus cash, no covenant pressure and a stable ten-year requirement, the on-premise route becomes cheaper beyond year five, since a perpetual licence keeps running while subscriptions do not stop.

body.title: Check your own spending decisions
steps: List your team's three largest spending proposals for the year and tag each as capex or opex.
For each capex item, find the useful life your company applies and work out the annual depreciation.
Check which of your proposals hit EBITDA and which sit below it.
For any capex, estimate how much it adds to capital employed and what that does to ROCE.
Ask finance whether training, trial runs or early running costs in your project are being expensed rather than capitalised.
Where a lease or subscription is an option, compare total cash over the full life, not just the annual figure.

cards.definition: Spending that creates an asset with benefit beyond the current period. Capitalised, then depreciated.
Spending consumed within the period, charged to the P&L immediately.
Recording spending as an asset rather than an expense.
Capitalised spending on an asset not yet ready for use, on which depreciation has not started.
The amount expected at the end of an asset's useful life, commonly taken as 5% of cost.
Charging an equal amount each year over the asset's useful life.
Depreciation applied to intangible assets such as software licences.

points: Capex creates an asset and reaches the P&L slowly through depreciation. Opex hits profit immediately.
The test is whether the spending produces benefit beyond the current period, and repairs are opex while upgrades are capex.
An asset's cost includes freight, installation and directly attributable costs, but not training, overheads or early operating losses.
Depreciation starts only when an asset is ready for use, which is why delayed projects sit in capital work in progress.
Capex leaves EBITDA untouched but raises capital employed and depresses ROCE until the asset performs.
Choose between buying and subscribing on cash position, obsolescence risk and total cost over the full life, and say which constraint drove the choice.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the Pune auto components maker are fictional, and all prices are illustrative. Schedule II lives are indicative and a company may use a different life with justification, so confirm your own company's policy with finance. Lease accounting under Ind AS 116 may require some arrangements described here as subscriptions to be recognised on the balance sheet.
